column9: "25 m/s north" is an example of –
column28: 25 m/s north gives a speed AND a direction, so it is a velocity. A speed would be just 25 m/s with no direction.
column29: Look for the part that tells which way the object is going.

column9: Speed and velocity are the same thing because they have the same units.
column28: False. Velocity has the same units as speed, but velocity includes the direction of motion; speed does not.
column29: Units are the same, but what extra piece of information does velocity have?

column9: The momentum of an object is the product of its mass and its ___.
column28: Momentum = mass × velocity (p = m × v).
column29: Momentum uses how much stuff is moving and how fast it is going in a direction.

column9: Which symbol is used to represent momentum?
column28: Momentum is represented by the symbol p, so p = m × v. The letter m is mass and v is velocity.
column29: It is NOT the first letter of the word momentum, because that letter is already used for mass.

column9: What is the unit for momentum?
column28: Momentum = mass × velocity, so its unit is kg × m/s = kg·m/s. A common mistake is writing only m/s (that is velocity).
column29: Multiply the unit for mass by the unit for velocity.

column9: Match each quantity to its unit.
column28: Mass is in kg, velocity in m/s (same units as speed), momentum in kg·m/s, time in s, and distance in m.
column29: Momentum's unit is mass's unit times velocity's unit.

column9: A car drives around a curve at a constant 35 mi/h. Which of these stays constant?
column28: The speed stays 35 mi/h, but the direction keeps changing on the curve, so the velocity is NOT constant. Only the speed is constant.
column29: Velocity includes direction. Does the car's direction change on a curve?

column9: A velocity can be negative, but a speed is never negative.
column28: True. Speed is just how fast (always positive or zero). Velocity includes direction, so a negative sign can show the opposite direction (like west or backward).
column29: Which one only tells how fast, and which one also tells which way?

column9: Which of these is a velocity?
column28: 12 m/s east has a speed and a direction, so it is a velocity. 60 km/h is only a speed, 300 m is a distance, and 50 kg·m/s is a momentum.
column29: A velocity needs a speed unit AND a direction.

column9: A 1,200 kg car is moving at 25 m/s. What is its momentum? Answer in kg·m/s.
column28: Formula: p = m × v. Set Up: p = 1,200 kg × 25 m/s. Answer: 30,000 kg·m/s.
column29: Momentum = mass × velocity. Multiply.

column9: An object is in motion if its position changes compared to a ___ point.
column28: A reference point is the object you compare position to. If the distance from the reference point changes, the object is moving.
column29: It is the object you compare against to decide whether something moved.

column9: A car, a bicycle, a mouse, and a bug all have the same velocity. Which has the greatest momentum?
column28: With the same velocity, the object with the most mass has the most momentum (p = m × v). The car has the most mass.
column29: If velocity is the same for all four, which part of p = m × v is different?

column9: An object that is sitting still has zero momentum.
column28: True. Sitting still means velocity = 0 m/s, and p = m × 0 = 0 kg·m/s, no matter how big the mass is.
column29: Plug a velocity of 0 into p = m × v.

column9: Which TWO quantities do you need to know to calculate an object's momentum? Select all that apply.
column28: p = m × v, so you need mass and velocity. Time and distance are used for speed, not directly for momentum.
column29: Think of the momentum formula: p = ? × ?

column9: Velocity has the same units as –
column28: Velocity has the same units as speed (like m/s or mi/h). The only difference is that velocity also gives a direction.
column29: Velocity is a speed with a direction added.

column9: Marcus has a mass of 65 kg and runs at 4.2 m/s. What is his momentum? Answer in kg·m/s.
column28: Formula: p = m × v. Set Up: p = 65 kg × 4.2 m/s. Answer: 273 kg·m/s.
column29: Momentum = mass × velocity. Write the formula first, then plug in.

column9: A 22.5 kg dog runs east with a momentum of 81 kg·m/s. Its velocity is ___ m/s east. What number goes in the blank?
column28: Formula: v = p / m. Set Up: v = 81 kg·m/s ÷ 22.5 kg. Answer: 3.6 m/s. A common mistake is multiplying instead of dividing.
column29: Velocity = momentum / mass. Which number goes on top?

column9: A deer has a momentum of 420 kg·m/s and is running at 6.0 m/s. What is the deer's mass? Answer in kg.
column28: Formula: m = p / v. Set Up: m = 420 kg·m/s ÷ 6.0 m/s. Answer: 70 kg.
column29: Mass = momentum / velocity.

column9: Ava rides her bike 1,500 m east in 300 s. Her velocity is ___ m/s east. What number goes in the blank?
column28: Formula: v = d / t. Set Up: v = 1,500 m ÷ 300 s. Answer: 5 m/s east.
column29: Velocity = distance / time, then add the direction.

column9: Jae walks 120 m north in 60 s. What is his velocity?
column28: Formula: v = d / t. Set Up: v = 120 m ÷ 60 s. Answer: 2 m/s north. Choice A is only a speed because it leaves out the direction.
column29: Divide distance by time, and remember velocity needs a direction.

column9: Two identical 1,000 kg cars drive down Highway 29. Car A goes 15 m/s and Car B goes 25 m/s. Which statement is true?
column14: Car A has more momentum because it is slower.
column15: They have the same momentum because they have the same mass.
column16: Car B has more momentum because it is faster.
column17: Neither car has momentum because they are on a highway.
column28: Same mass, different velocity: the faster car has more momentum. Car B: 1,000 × 25 = 25,000 kg·m/s vs Car A: 15,000 kg·m/s.
column29: The masses are equal, so which part of p = m × v decides?

column9: A pickup truck and a small car drive side by side on Broadway at the same velocity. Which has more momentum?
column14: The car, because it is smaller and easier to move
column15: They have the same momentum because they have the same velocity
column16: The car, because small objects go farther
column17: The truck, because it has more mass
column28: Same velocity, so the object with more mass has more momentum. The truck has more mass, so it has more momentum.
column29: Which part of p = m × v is different between the two vehicles?

column9: A sled keeps the same mass, but its velocity triples. What happens to its momentum?
column28: p = m × v. If v is 3 times as big and m stays the same, p is 3 times as big.
column29: Try it with numbers: 1 kg × 1 m/s, then 1 kg × 3 m/s.

column9: A slow-moving truck can have more momentum than a fast-moving bicycle.
column28: True. Momentum depends on mass AND velocity. A 9,000 kg truck at 2 m/s has 18,000 kg·m/s; a 90 kg bike and rider at 10 m/s has only 900 kg·m/s.
column29: Momentum is not just about speed. What else is in p = m × v?

column9: Liv rolls a 7.0 kg bowling ball down the lane at 5.5 m/s. What is the ball's momentum? Answer in kg·m/s.
column28: Formula: p = m × v. Set Up: p = 7.0 kg × 5.5 m/s. Answer: 38.5 kg·m/s.
column29: Momentum = mass × velocity.

column9: A 15 kg shopping cart has a momentum of 27 kg·m/s. How fast is it moving? Answer in m/s.
column28: Formula: v = p / m. Set Up: v = 27 kg·m/s ÷ 15 kg. Answer: 1.8 m/s.
column29: Velocity = momentum / mass.

column9: A kicked soccer ball moves at 24 m/s and has a momentum of 10.8 kg·m/s. What is the ball's mass? Answer in kg.
column28: Formula: m = p / v. Set Up: m = 10.8 kg·m/s ÷ 24 m/s. Answer: 0.45 kg. If you got 259.2, you multiplied instead of dividing.
column29: Mass = momentum / velocity.

column9: A train travels at a constant velocity of 90 km/h east for 2.5 hours. How far does it travel? Answer in km.
column28: Formula: d = v × t. Set Up: d = 90 km/h × 2.5 h. Answer: 225 km (east).
column29: Distance = speed × time. Check that the time units match (hours with km/h).

column9: Put the steps for solving a momentum problem in order (Formula / Set Up / Answer).
column14: Plug the known values into the formula with their units.
column15: Write the final answer with units of kg·m/s.
column28: Formula first (p = m × v), then Set Up by plugging in mass and velocity with units, then multiply, then write the answer with units (kg·m/s).
column29: Mr. Erickson's method: Formula, then Set Up, then Answer with units.

column9: Maya is sitting in her seat on a moving school bus. Compared to which reference point is Maya NOT moving?
column16: The seat in front of her
column28: Maya stays the same distance from the seat in front of her, so compared to it she is not moving. Compared to a tree, a stop sign, or a parked car, her position changes.
column29: Pick the object that is moving along with Maya.

column9: A car stays at 35 mi/h while it turns a corner. Its speed does not change, but its velocity changes because its ___ changes. (A change in velocity is called acceleration.)
column28: Velocity is speed plus direction. Turning changes the direction, so the velocity changes even at a constant speed. Any change in velocity is acceleration.
column29: What does velocity include that speed does not?

column9: Match each change to what happens to the object's momentum.
column14: Mass doubles, velocity stays the same :: Momentum doubles
column15: Velocity is cut in half, mass stays the same :: Momentum is cut in half
column16: The object stops :: Momentum becomes zero
column17: Mass and velocity both double :: Momentum becomes 4 times as large
column28: p = m × v. Doubling the mass doubles p; halving v halves p; v = 0 makes p = 0; doubling both makes p 2 × 2 = 4 times as large.
column29: Try each one with numbers, starting from 1 kg × 1 m/s.

column9: Kellen drives his scooter down Myrtle Street for 5 minutes and travels 1.2 miles heading north. His velocity is ___ miles per minute north. What number goes in the blank?
column28: Formula: v = d / t. Set Up: v = 1.2 mi ÷ 5 min. Answer: 0.24 mi/min north.
column29: Velocity = distance / time. Divide miles by minutes.

column9: Ball X has a mass of 2 kg and moves at 10 m/s. Ball Y has a mass of 10 kg and moves at 2 m/s. Which has more momentum?
column14: Ball X, because it is faster
column15: Ball Y, because it is heavier
column28: Ball X: 2 kg × 10 m/s = 20 kg·m/s. Ball Y: 10 kg × 2 m/s = 20 kg·m/s. They have the same momentum.
column29: Calculate p = m × v for each ball before choosing.

column9: A 145 g baseball is thrown at 40 m/s. What is its momentum? Answer in kg·m/s. (Watch units: 1 kg = 1,000 g.)
column28: Convert first: 145 g × (1 kg / 1,000 g) = 0.145 kg. Formula: p = m × v. Set Up: p = 0.145 kg × 40 m/s. Answer: 5.8 kg·m/s. Using 145 instead of 0.145 gives an answer 1,000 times too big.
column29: Change grams to kilograms before you use p = m × v.

column9: A 1,400 kg car drives east at 54 km/h. What is its momentum? Answer in kg·m/s. (Watch units: 1 km = 1,000 m and 1 h = 3,600 s.)
column28: Convert first: 54 km/h × 1,000 m/km ÷ 3,600 s/h = 15 m/s. Formula: p = m × v. Set Up: p = 1,400 kg × 15 m/s. Answer: 21,000 kg·m/s (east).
column29: Momentum must use m/s. Change km/h to m/s first: multiply by 1,000 and divide by 3,600.

column9: Riley runs 3.0 km north in 12.5 minutes. Her velocity is ___ m/s north. What number goes in the blank? (Watch units: 1 km = 1,000 m and 1 min = 60 s.)
column28: Convert: 3.0 km = 3,000 m and 12.5 min × 60 = 750 s. Formula: v = d / t. Set Up: v = 3,000 m ÷ 750 s. Answer: 4 m/s north.
column29: Change km to m and minutes to seconds before dividing.

column9: A 50 kg skater glides 120 m east in 20 s at a constant velocity. What is the skater's momentum? Answer in kg·m/s.
column28: Step 1: v = d / t = 120 m ÷ 20 s = 6 m/s east. Step 2: p = m × v = 50 kg × 6 m/s. Answer: 300 kg·m/s (east).
column29: You need the velocity first. Use v = d / t, then p = m × v.

column9: A lab cart rolls 36 m in 9.0 s at a constant velocity and has a momentum of 60 kg·m/s. What is the cart's mass? Answer in kg.
column28: Step 1: v = d / t = 36 m ÷ 9.0 s = 4 m/s. Step 2: m = p / v = 60 kg·m/s ÷ 4 m/s. Answer: 15 kg.
column29: Find the velocity from the distance and time, then use m = p / v.

column9: An 8,100 kg dump truck moves at 10 m/s. A 1,500 kg car moves at 18 m/s. How many times greater is the truck's momentum than the car's?
column29: Find p = m × v for each vehicle, then divide the larger by the smaller.

column9: A 6,000 kg truck moves at 4.0 m/s. How fast would a 1,500 kg car have to move to have the same momentum as the truck? Answer in m/s.
column28: Truck: p = 6,000 kg × 4.0 m/s = 24,000 kg·m/s. Car: v = p / m = 24,000 kg·m/s ÷ 1,500 kg. Answer: 16 m/s.
column29: Find the truck's momentum first. Then use v = p / m with the car's mass.

column9: Enrichment: Cart A (3.0 kg) rolls at 4.0 m/s and hits Cart B (3.0 kg), which is at rest. The carts stick together. Momentum is conserved in the collision. What is the total momentum of the carts after the collision? Answer in kg·m/s.
column28: Before: p = 3.0 kg × 4.0 m/s + 3.0 kg × 0 m/s = 12 kg·m/s. Momentum is conserved, so total momentum after = 12 kg·m/s.
column29: Cart B is at rest, so its momentum is zero. Total before = total after.

column9: Enrichment: A 2 kg cart moving east at 9 m/s hits a 1 kg cart at rest. They stick together and move as one. Momentum is conserved. What is the velocity of the two carts together after the collision? (They move east; give the number in m/s.)
column28: Before: p = 2 kg × 9 m/s = 18 kg·m/s. After: same momentum, mass = 2 kg + 1 kg = 3 kg. v = p / m = 18 ÷ 3 = 6 m/s.
column29: Find the total momentum before. After, the carts move together, so use their combined mass in v = p / m.

column9: A jet flies at a constant velocity of 240 m/s west for 2.5 minutes. How far does it travel? Answer in m. (Watch units: 1 min = 60 s.)
column28: Convert: 2.5 min × 60 = 150 s. Formula: d = v × t. Set Up: d = 240 m/s × 150 s. Answer: 36,000 m (west).
column29: Change minutes to seconds so the units match m/s, then use d = v × t.

column9: Object A and Object B have the same momentum. Object A has 3 times the mass of Object B. Which statement is true?
column14: Object B moves 3 times as fast as Object A.
column15: Object A moves 3 times as fast as Object B.
column16: They move at the same velocity.
column17: Object B moves one-third as fast as Object A.
column28: p = m × v is the same for both. If A has 3 times the mass, B must have 3 times the velocity to make the same product.
column29: Try numbers: A = 3 kg, B = 1 kg, and both have p = 6 kg·m/s.

column9: Jae is on a train moving 20 m/s east. He walks toward the front of the train at 2 m/s east, compared to the train. What is Jae's velocity compared to the ground?
column28: Compared to the ground, Jae moves with the train AND walks forward in the same direction: 20 m/s + 2 m/s = 22 m/s east.
column29: Both motions point east. Do they add or subtract?

column9: Which of these objects have a momentum of exactly 120 kg·m/s? Select all that apply.
column17: A 30 kg child on a bike at 5 m/s
column29: Multiply mass × velocity for each choice.

column9: A cart's mass is cut in half and its velocity triples. What happens to its momentum?
column28: New p = (½ m) × (3 v) = 1.5 × m × v. The momentum becomes 1.5 times as large. Example: 2 kg × 1 m/s = 2; 1 kg × 3 m/s = 3, which is 1.5 times 2.
column29: Try numbers: start with 2 kg × 1 m/s, then use 1 kg × 3 m/s and compare.

column9: Use east as positive and west as negative. A cyclist rides 480 m west in 80 s. What is her velocity in m/s? (Include the sign.)
column28: Formula: v = d / t. Set Up: v = 480 m ÷ 80 s = 6 m/s, and the direction is west, so v = -6 m/s. Her speed is 6 m/s, but her velocity is negative because she moves west.
column29: Find how fast first, then use the sign to show the direction.

column9: Andrea found the mass of a dog with p = 90 kg·m/s and v = 3 m/s. She wrote: m = 90 × 3 = 270 kg. What should she have done?
column16: Divided the other way: m = 3 ÷ 90 = 0.033 kg
column28: Mass = momentum / velocity, so she should divide: m = 90 kg·m/s ÷ 3 m/s = 30 kg. Multiplying is only for finding p.
column29: Look at the formula triangle: p is on top, m and v are on the bottom.
